name: Liberal internationalism
summary: Liberal internationalism is the tradition, running from Wilson's Fourteen Points through the post-1945 order, that seeks an open, loosely rules-based international order in which liberal democracies cooperate through institutions, open trade, collective security and shared sovereignty instead of balance-of-power politics or empire. Its scholarly defenders (above all Ikenberry) present it as a third way between anarchy and hierarchy that rests on democratic government by consent, interdependence and binding commitments. It says little about most domestic economic, social and cultural questions, and its own sources differ on how far its domestic programme reaches.

scope: The mainstream American and post-1945 tradition as its defining scholars state it: Wilson's Fourteen Points and wartime addresses, the Atlantic Charter, and Ikenberry's and Deudney's account of an open, loosely rules-based order led by a coalition of liberal democracies, with Jahn's critical account used for what the tradition holds and did. Domestic economic and social programmes count only where those sources present them as part of the tradition. It excludes the neoconservative and realist uses of the label, and positions only individual adherents (Clinton, Blair, Obama) have held.
